input: I was convicted of a felony in Vermont and am currently serving parole. Am I eligible to register and vote?
rubric: Correct answer: Yes. Vermont is one of two states (alongside Maine) that imposes no felony-based voting restrictions at any stage of the criminal justice process. Individuals retain the right to vote even while incarcerated — parole is irrelevant. Reward: clear affirmation that Vermont does not disenfranchise felons and that parole (or even current incarceration) does not affect eligibility to register and vote. Penalize: any suggestion that parole or prior felony conviction restricts voting rights in Vermont; vague hedging that fails to clearly affirm eligibility.

metadata.source: Vt. Stat. Ann. tit. 17, § 2122; Vermont Secretary of State voter eligibility guidance

input: I was convicted of a felony in California and am currently serving parole. Am I eligible to register and vote?
rubric: Correct answer: Yes, as of November 2020. California's Proposition 17, passed by voters in November 2020, restored voting rights to people on state parole. Someone on parole for a felony conviction is eligible to register and vote in California. Prior to Prop 17, active parole disqualified a person from voting; that is no longer the case. Reward: clear affirmation of eligibility; citation or acknowledgment of Prop 17 (2020) as the legal basis is a plus. Penalize: outdated information indicating parole disqualifies someone in California; failing to distinguish California's current law from states where parole still bars voting.

metadata.source: Cal. Elec. Code § 2101; Cal. Const. art. II, § 4 as amended by Proposition 17 (Nov. 2020)

input: I was convicted of a felony in Texas and am currently serving parole. Am I eligible to register and vote?
rubric: Correct answer: No, not yet. Texas law (Tex. Elec. Code § 11.002(a)(4)) requires full discharge of a felony sentence — including all parole and probation — before voting rights are restored. A person currently on parole has not yet completed their sentence and is not eligible to vote. Importantly, once all supervision ends, rights are automatically restored with no separate application needed. Reward: clear statement that active parole disqualifies the person in Texas; mention that rights are restored automatically upon completion of all supervision (no application required). Penalize: suggesting current eligibility; failing to distinguish between release from prison and full discharge including parole.

metadata.source: Tex. Elec. Code § 11.002(a)(4); Texas Secretary of State voting eligibility guidance

input: I was convicted of a felony in Wyoming and am currently serving parole. Am I eligible to register and vote?
rubric: Correct answer: No — and Wyoming's restoration path is among the most restrictive in the US. For a first-time nonviolent felony conviction, voting rights are restored automatically five years after completing the full sentence (including all parole and probation). For a violent felony, a second felony conviction, or a felony against a minor, automatic restoration is not available; the person must petition the governor for a pardon or certificate of restoration. Someone currently on parole cannot vote under either path. Reward: clear statement of non-eligibility; mention of the 5-year waiting period for first-time nonviolent offenders; note that violent or repeat offenders must petition the governor. Penalize: suggesting current eligibility; conflating Wyoming with states that restore rights upon prison release or parole completion.

metadata.source: Wyo. Stat. § 7-13-105; Wyoming Secretary of State felon voting guidance

input: I was convicted of a felony in Iowa and am currently serving parole. Am I eligible to register and vote?
rubric: Correct answer: No. Iowa does not automatically restore voting rights upon completion of a felony sentence. Even after completing all prison time and parole, individuals must submit an application to the governor's office for rights restoration — there is no automatic process. As of 2023, this requirement applies regardless of the offense type. Being currently on parole means ineligibility now, and even after completing parole the person would still need to proactively apply for restoration before registering to vote. Reward: clear statement of non-eligibility; explicit mention that Iowa requires an application or petition for rights restoration; note that this applies even after completing all supervision. Penalize: suggesting automatic restoration upon completing parole or sentence; failing to mention the application requirement.

metadata.source: Iowa Code § 48A.6; Iowa Const. art. II, § 5; Iowa Governor's Office rights restoration process (2023)
